titleText.es: Es todavía más difícil si eres el típico capullo que pronuncia los caracteres <>.
titleText.en: It's even harder if you're an asshole who pronounces <> brackets.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text. It calls the angle-bracket characters caracteres, while the official English wording calls them brackets; the joke depends on how code symbols are pronounced when counting a haiku's rhythm.

regions.labelEs: SEÑALES DE QUE VUESTROS PROGRAMADORES NO TIENEN MUCHO TRABAJO QUE HACER.

applications.explanationEn: Vuestros is the informal-plural ‘your’ form used mainly in Spain; its masculine plural ending matches programadores.
Trabajo names what is pending, que links it to the action, and hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

excludedUnits.rationale: Gopher is the unchanged proper name of an Internet protocol, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

All three words form the fixed precaution expression; none is translated separately in natural English.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the irregular positive tú command of oír and is used here to get one familiar person's attention.
Habéis is the informal-plural helper used mainly in Spain, and visto is the completed-action form that follows it.
Habéis is the present-perfect helper for vosotros or vosotras, addressing several familiar people in the form common in Spain.

cards.noteEn: Here señales means clues or indications that suggest something is true, not road signs or posted notices.

example.es: Hay señales de que todo mejora.
example.en: There are signs that everything is improving.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links señales to the evidence that follows
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses de before que after señal or señales when the following clause states what the sign indicates. English normally expresses the combination as ‘a sign that...’ without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una señal de que funciona.
example.en: It is a sign that it works.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before masculine plural things)

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.questionEn: How can a noun name something available, pending, or necessary to do?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the noun, then use the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs mean ‘followed by,’ sustantivo means a noun, and infinitivo means the unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. Common examples include trabajo que hacer, algo que leer, and nada que decir.

example.en: There is a report to finish.

cards.answerEn: to; links a noun to an action available or needing to be done
cards.noteEn: After a noun such as trabajo, algo, or nada, que can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form. Natural English often uses ‘to’ instead.

example.en: We have several tasks to finish.

cards.noteEn: Casi goes before the word or action that comes close to being true but is not fully complete.

example.en: I have almost finished.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Recuperado is the completed-action form of recuperar. With haber it says that a previous ability, level, or possession has been regained.

example.en: I have regained my previous pace.

cards.noteEn: Before a noun, antiguo or antigua can mean the earlier or former version of something rather than something ancient.

example.en: She returned to her former routine.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Escritura usually means writing. In a computing context, velocidad de escritura is the speed at which someone types.

example.es: Su escritura es más rápida con este teclado.
example.en: Her typing is faster with this keyboard.

cards.answerEn: using; in (a keyboard layout or system)
cards.noteEn: With the name of a keyboard layout, en identifies the system being used. Natural English often says ‘using’ that layout.

example.en: She types using QWERTY.

cards.noteEn: Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.

example.en: Our computers work well.

cards.questionEn: How do you choose the Spanish form of ‘our’ before a noun?
cards.answerEn: Choose nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, or nuestras to match the gender and number of what is owned.
cards.noteEn: The form matches the owned noun, not the owners. Use nuestro before one masculine thing, nuestra before one feminine thing, nuestros before masculine or mixed plural things, and nuestras before feminine plural things.

example.en: Our suitcases are here.

cards.noteEn: In computing, a servidor is a computer or program that provides data or services to other computers.

example.es: Los servidores alojan la página web.
example.en: The servers host the website.

cards.answerEn: they support; they are compatible with
cards.noteEn: In a technical context, soportar means that a system can work with a protocol, format, or feature. It is not the physical sense of holding something up.

example.en: These browsers support the format.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si acaso, ‘just in case’
cards.noteEn: Por is fixed inside the three-word precaution expression por si acaso.

example.en: Take water just in case.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that you take a precaution “just in case”?
cards.answerEn: Use por si acaso after the precaution.
cards.noteEn: Por si acaso is a fixed expression for preparing for something uncertain. A shorter por si + clause can name the possibility directly, as in por si llueve, ‘in case it rains.’

example.en: I'm bringing money just in case.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of por si acaso, ‘just in case’
cards.noteEn: Si remains unaccented inside por si acaso. The whole expression introduces a precaution for an uncertain possibility.

example.es: Trae una chaqueta por si acaso.
example.en: Bring a jacket just in case.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por si acaso, ‘just in case’
cards.noteEn: Acaso completes the fixed precaution expression. This is different from acaso used by itself to add doubt to a question.

example.es: Guarda una copia por si acaso.
example.en: Keep a copy just in case.

cards.answerEn: A haiku is a Japanese poetic form commonly taught outside Japan as three short lines following a 5–7–5 rhythm; the comic jokes that HTML markup can satisfy both code rules and poetic form.
cards.noteEn: The title text adds that the count becomes harder when angle brackets are pronounced aloud, making the way code symbols are read part of the joke.
Cumplen is a plural form of cumplir. With con, it says that several things meet a rule, requirement, or standard.

example.es: Las páginas cumplen con la norma.
example.en: The pages meet the standard.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something meets a requirement or standard?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of cumplir, then con, then name the requirement or standard.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means ‘followed by.’ Cumplir changes to match its subject, while con stays unchanged: cumple con for one thing and cumplen con for several things.

example.es: El diseño cumple con la norma.
example.en: The design meets the standard.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; links cumplir to a requirement or standard
cards.noteEn: Cumplir con introduces the rule, promise, requirement, or standard that is met. English often uses ‘meet’ directly with no word for con.

example.es: El producto cumple con los requisitos.
example.en: The product meets the requirements.

cards.answerEn: haiku; a short Japanese poetic form
cards.noteEn: Haiku is used in Spanish for the Japanese poetic form. Here it names the poem type, not the Haiku operating system.

example.es: Escribió un haiku sobre la lluvia.
example.en: She wrote a haiku about the rain.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Habéis is the present helper form of haber used with vosotros or vosotras. It comes before a completed-action form such as llegado or oído.

example.en: You all have arrived early.

cards.noteEn: Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

example.en: We have seen that movie.

cards.answerEn: webcomic; comic published on the web
cards.noteEn: Webcómic combines web with cómic. Standard Spanish spelling keeps the written accent because the stressed syllable remains có.

example.en: She reads a webcomic every week.
